prompt: What reagents are used, in order, in the Edman degradation?

choices.why: PITC must first attach to the N-terminal –NH2 group; the acid then splits off the terminal residue.

choices.text: Ninhydrin in aqueous NaOH, then iodoacetic acid
choices.why: Ninhydrin is used to detect amino acids in amino acid analysis, not to sequence peptides.

choices.text: Aqueous 6 M HCl at 110 °C for 24 hours
choices.why: These conditions hydrolyze all the amide bonds for amino acid analysis, which destroys the sequence information.

explanation: Edman degradation treats a peptide with phenyl isothiocyanate (PITC), C6H5–N=C=S, followed by trifluoroacetic acid. The first step attaches PITC to the N-terminal –NH2 group, and the second splits off the N-terminal residue.

prompt: Which residue does each cycle of the Edman degradation remove from a peptide?

choices.why: PITC attaches to the free –NH2 group, so the residue removed is at the N-terminal end.

choices.text: Any residue next to Arg or Lys
choices.why: That describes cleavage by trypsin, not the Edman degradation.

choices.text: A random residue, because the acid step is unselective
choices.why: Edman degradation cleaves one amino acid at a time from the N-terminal end; it is acid hydrolysis that is unselective.

explanation: The first step of the Edman degradation attaches PITC to the –NH2 group of the N-terminal amino acid, and the second step splits that N-terminal residue from the chain. The chain-shortened peptide is then resubmitted for another cycle.

prompt: In the Edman degradation, what happens to the anilinothiazolinone (ATZ) derivative of the cleaved residue?

choices.text: Aqueous acid rearranges it to a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH), which is identified by its elution time
It is hydrolyzed back to the free amino acid, which is identified by its ninhydrin color
choices.why: The ATZ is converted into a PTH derivative, which is identified by comparing elution times with known PTH derivatives.

choices.text: It reattaches to the chain-shortened peptide for the next cycle
choices.why: The chain-shortened peptide goes on to the next cycle; the ATZ is converted into a PTH for identification.

choices.text: It is identified directly by its molecular weight in Table 26.1.1
choices.why: The ATZ is first converted into a PTH, which is identified by elution time.

explanation: Cleavage gives an anilinothiazolinone (ATZ) derivative plus the chain-shortened peptide. Further acid-catalyzed rearrangement with aqueous acid converts the ATZ into a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH), identified by comparing its elution time with those of the PTH derivatives of the 20 common amino acids.

prompt: Automated protein sequencers can carry out as many as how many repetitive Edman cycles before by-products interfere with the results?
explanation: Automated sequencers allow as many as 50 repetitive cycles before a buildup of unwanted by-products interferes. For this reason, large proteins are first partially hydrolyzed into smaller fragments, which are sequenced and fitted together by their overlapping ends.

prompt: Angiotensin II has the sequence Asp-Arg-Val-Tyr-Ile-His-Pro-Phe. What fragments form when it is cleaved with chymotrypsin?

choices.why: These are the trypsin fragments, from cleavage on the carboxyl side of Arg.
Chymotrypsin cleaves on the carboxyl side of the aryl-substituted residue, so Tyr stays at the end of the first fragment.
Chymotrypsin doesn't cleave next to His; it cleaves after Phe, Tyr, and Trp.

explanation: Chymotrypsin cleaves only at the carboxyl side of the aryl-substituted amino acids phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan. Angiotensin II is cut after Tyr; Phe is already the C-terminal residue. The fragments are Asp-Arg-Val-Tyr and Ile-His-Pro-Phe (Exercise 26.6.1).

prompt: Angiotensin II has the sequence Asp-Arg-Val-Tyr-Ile-His-Pro-Phe. What fragments form when it is cleaved with trypsin?

choices.why: Trypsin cleaves on the carboxyl side of Arg, so Arg stays with Asp.
These are the chymotrypsin fragments, from cleavage after Tyr.
Trypsin cleaves only after the basic residues Arg and Lys; His is not one of them.

explanation: Trypsin catalyzes hydrolysis only at the carboxyl side of arginine and lysine. Angiotensin II has one such residue, Arg, so trypsin gives Asp-Arg and Val-Tyr-Ile-His-Pro-Phe (Exercise 26.6.1).

prompt: Angiotensin II (Asp-Arg-Val-Tyr-Ile-His-Pro-Phe) undergoes one cycle of Edman degradation. From which amino acid is the PTH derivative formed?

choices.why: Phe is the C-terminal residue; the Edman degradation removes the N-terminal residue.
Arg is the second residue; it is removed in the second cycle.
Pro is next to the C-terminal end; Edman degradation works from the N-terminal end.

explanation: The Edman degradation removes the N-terminal residue, which is written on the left. For angiotensin II that is Asp, so the first PTH derivative is that of aspartic acid; its side chain carries an acetic acid residue, –CH2CO2H (Exercise 26.6.3).

prompt: A hexapeptide containing Arg, Gly, Ile, Leu, Pro, and Val gives the fragments Pro-Leu-Gly, Arg-Pro, and Gly-Ile-Val on partial acid hydrolysis. What is its sequence?

choices.why: This sequence has no Arg-Pro link, so it can't give the Arg-Pro fragment.
Here Leu is C-terminal with no Gly after it, so the Pro-Leu-Gly fragment can't form.
This sequence has no Pro-Leu link, so it can't give the Pro-Leu-Gly fragment.

explanation: Fit the fragments by their overlapping ends: Arg-Pro overlaps Pro-Leu-Gly at Pro, and Pro-Leu-Gly overlaps Gly-Ile-Val at Gly. That gives Arg-Pro-Leu-Gly-Ile-Val (Exercise 26.6.4).

prompt: A hexapeptide with the composition N, L, M, W, V2 gives the fragments V-L, V-M-W, and W-N-V on partial acid hydrolysis. What is its sequence?

choices.why: This is the right sequence read backward. Peptides are written from the N-terminal end, so the fragments V-M-W and W-N-V must read left to right.
This sequence has no W-N-V or V-L link, so it can't give those fragments.
Here Asn is C-terminal with no Val after it, so the W-N-V fragment can't form.

explanation: V-M-W overlaps W-N-V at W, giving V-M-W-N-V, and W-N-V overlaps V-L at the second V, giving V-M-W-N-V-L. In three-letter codes that is Val-Met-Trp-Asn-Val-Leu; N is asparagine (Exercise 26.6.4).

prompt: How many fragments form when the peptide Gly-Lys-Ala-Phe-Arg-Ser is completely cleaved with trypsin?
explanation: Trypsin cleaves only at the carboxyl side of Arg and Lys. This peptide is cut after Lys and after Arg, giving three fragments: Gly-Lys, Ala-Phe-Arg, and Ser.
